overview: This file consists of a two-page U.S. consular despatch from Taihoku reporting the fatal crash of a Japan Air Transport Company passenger aircraft at Giran in colonial Taiwan on June 24, 1938. The twin-motored East Coast service plane, identified by the press as the six-passenger “ENVOY (DOAX),” crashed while approaching Giran on its return from Taito, killing its pilot and four Japanese passengers. The despatch attributes the accident tentatively to a sudden gust of wind and places it in the context of two earlier fatal passenger-plane crashes at Fukuoka.

subfiles.title: Despatch on the fatal Japan Air Transport crash at Giran
subfiles.from: William E. Young, American Vice Consul, Taihoku
subfiles.to: The Secretary of State, Washington, D.C.
subfiles.about: Reports the June 24, 1938 crash of a Japan Air Transport Company passenger aircraft at Giran, Taiwan, which killed the pilot and four passengers.
subfiles.summary: The despatch states that a twin-motored passenger plane operating Japan Air Transport Company’s Taiwan East Coast route plunged to the ground near Giran while returning from Taito to Taihoku. The aircraft was destroyed, and its pilot and four Japanese passengers were killed instantly; a sudden gust of wind was suspected, although the cause remained unknown. Young describes it as the worst commercial aviation disaster yet recorded in Japan and compares it with fatal passenger-plane crashes at Fukuoka in 1931 and the preceding year.

interest: The despatch offers a compact contemporary account of an early commercial-aviation disaster within Japanese-ruled Taiwan, including the route, altitude, flight phase, casualty count, and the first tentative explanation of the crash. Its claim that this was Japan’s worst commercial air disaster to date, together with its references to the two earlier Fukuoka accidents, is useful for reconstructing how officials understood the safety record of Japanese passenger aviation. The document also illustrates how the U.S. consular network gathered local press reports and distributed information among the State Department, the embassy, and the consulate general in Tokyo.
